newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: N.Ireland talks under pressure after arms vote.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks under pressure after arms vote.

text.p: Britain and Ireland were struggling to keep Northern Ireland peace efforts on track on Thursday after Protestant politicians rejected key proposals on the surrender of guerrilla arms.

"It's clearly a setback, but I don't think it's a long-lasting setback," former U.S. senator George Mitchell, chairman of the province's peace talks, told reporters after Protestant unionist parties voted the plan down.
Belfast media said the vote cast grave doubts over the future of the talks process, but the Dublin media applauded Anglo-Irish determination to press ahead with negotiations.
"Further delay will kill the talks," said Belfast's nationalist Irish News, while the News Letter, read by unionists, asked: "Where do we go now?".
The Irish Times, published in Dublin, said the main Ulster Unionist Party may have disrupted the talks timetable but they must know that "the settlement train will not be derailed".
Meanwhile Northern Ireland police said they had found bomb-making equipment in a roadside ditch.
About eight kilos of explosives and eight coffee jars adapted to be used as bombs had been seized in the find at Pomeroy, County Tyrone on Wednesday.
The Irish Republican Army (IRA) has large quantities of arms and explosives in concealed stockpiles in Northern Ireland and in the Irish republic.
The arms decommissioning vote dashed hopes that a compromise was imminent on the surrender of guerrilla weapons after 14 months of deadlock and painstaking Anglo-Irish diplomacy.

The unionists, guardians of British rule of the province, rejected the plan because it would have allowed the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to take part in talks without surrendering any of its guns and bombs.

The IRA ordered a truce last weekend in its 28-year war against British rule, but unionists tended to dismiss it as a ploy to enable Sinn Fein to attend substantive peace negotiations due to start on September 15.

Two small unionist parties, the Democratic Unionists and the UK Unionists, walked out of the talks after the vote and the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party insisted that it would not negotiate with Sinn Fein while its IRA allies remain armed.

The unionists fear the IRA, one of the world's most experienced guerrilla organisations, will return to violence unless the talks lead to a united Ireland, a prospect which Northern Ireland's Protestants staunchly reject.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam and Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke pledged to press ahead with plans for political negotiations and would work for a compromise on surrendering guerrilla arms.
"The talks process goes on. Both governments are firmly committed to substantive political negotiations on 15 September," Mowlam said.
The two governments were backed by U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration which has supported Anglo-Irish attempts to reconcile unionists and catholics.
"We regret that vote," State Deparment spokesman James Foley told reporters. "I think the important point, though, is that the process will continue."

Mitchell said the talks would be formally adjourned until September after a session on Monday and hoped that a plan on surrendering weapons could be reached to allow the substantive negotiations to start.
